status: draft: open coding by Claude (claude-opus-5-5) on the 300-post sample, waiting for Nahuel's review
relevance_rule: Relevant = the post describes a problem someone has while building or running a software product as a team (any role). Not relevant: job ads, product launches with no problem stated, technical uses of the term (e.g. OS context switching), other domains.

codes.label: Code review is overloaded
codes.definition: Reviews are slow, clogged or shallow, often because of the volume or size of PRs (including AI-generated ones).

codes.label: AI-written code needs cleaning up
codes.definition: Code from AI tools is wrong, bloated or hard to maintain, and it creates rework or tech debt.

codes.label: Faster coding moved the bottleneck
codes.definition: Writing code got faster and the constraint moved downstream: review, QA, CI, design, product, ops or support can't keep up.

codes.label: Supervising agents is hard
codes.definition: Running, watching or trusting several AI agents takes attention, causes overload, or produces output that can't be trusted unattended.

codes.label: Interruptions and context switching
codes.definition: Pings, meetings or switching between tools and tasks break people's focus.

codes.label: Flaky tests and slow CI
codes.definition: Tests that fail randomly, break on small UI changes, or CI that takes too long to give an answer.

codes.label: Not enough QA
codes.definition: No QA, too little QA time, the manual testing load, or back-and-forth between QA and development.

codes.label: Vague or changing requirements
codes.definition: Requirements are unclear, incomplete or keep changing, so work is redone or estimates are wrong.

codes.label: Decisions happen too late
codes.definition: Whether the right thing was built only gets discussed at review or after the build. Requirements get handed over instead of being understood.

codes.label: Code drifts from the design system
codes.definition: The UI in code drifts from the design system or Figma. AI tools don't follow it either.

codes.label: Design and engineering work apart
codes.definition: Design and engineering work in separate tools, and handoffs between them lose information.

codes.label: Knowledge lives in people's heads
codes.definition: Docs are missing or outdated, knowledge sits with a few people, onboarding is slow.

codes.label: AI tools lack the team's context
codes.definition: AI tools don't know the team's conventions, docs, decisions or codebase rules, so people repeat them or fix the output.

codes.label: Tech debt never gets prioritised
codes.definition: Tech debt and quality work keep losing out to features.

codes.label: Status reporting is overhead
codes.definition: Standups, status updates and tracking for different audiences take time and nobody gets value from them.

codes.label: Too many tools
codes.definition: Work is spread across too many tools, or tools don't fit the team's process or partners.

codes.label: Non-engineers depend on engineering
codes.definition: People outside engineering can't make product changes themselves and wait for engineering, or are kept out of the code.

codes.label: Checks get skipped to go faster
codes.definition: Pressure to ship skips steps that protect quality: design review, copy review, brand checks, testing.

codes.label: Small changes have unexpected effects
codes.definition: A change spreads further than expected (to other files, services, tests or configs) and breaks something, or nobody can tell what a change will affect.

codes.label: Customer feedback doesn't reach the product team
codes.definition: Feedback from customers, sales or support doesn't get to the product team, gets lost, or gets ignored.

codes.label: Other
codes.definition: A relevant pain that doesn't fit any code above. Collected so the next version of the codebook can add codes.
